title: The Door and the Dream
relation: Siblings divided by an unseen refuge and a necessary seal
summary: Solarius and Nythea remember different fronts of the same disaster. He stood where the Sundering breached the First Concord; she sheltered mortal survivors where waking sight could not follow. The siblings once trusted daylight and dreaming to protect the same lives. Their estrangement begins with what each could not see, but neither account belongs to the other to finish. Their independent stories can be heard without serving as messenger or choosing a favored sibling.

aa: Judgment and Stillness bring the siblings to an account with two kinds of silence. Solarius withdraws his accusation that Nythea abandoned mortal life. Nythea declines to fill the missing sleepers' silence with imagined consent. He wants a complete list before speaking publicly; she points out that completeness has become another condition the dead cannot satisfy. Your two choices have made precision necessary, but neither god may use precision to postpone an admission indefinitely.

At this conversation, they agree on a sentence each can repeat without borrowing the other's authority: the breach was sealed while a refuge still held people beyond daylight's reach. Solarius can defend the necessity of his act without pronouncing on every person its timing stranded. Nythea can describe the lives she protected without certifying the fate of every sleeper. They do not call this reconciliation. She still hears the old accusation when he falls quiet; he still hears the absent defenders when she speaks of rescue. Yet their disagreement now has boundaries. A mortal asking what happened will no longer be required to inherit an accusation as the price of hearing about courage.
ab: Judgment and Defiance do not produce a gentle meeting. Solarius asks why Nythea promised a return she could not guarantee. Nythea asks why he turned a battlefield inference into an enduring charge. Neither question is answered by naming the lives its speaker saved. Your paths leave both siblings without their favorite defense: that effective protection grants its author the final word about everyone it affected.

Nythea says that a refuge must allow its survivors to describe confinement. Solarius says that a necessary seal must still be examined by those who were outside it. They disagree over what a better decision could have looked like during the Sundering. No hidden vision settles the argument, and nobody offers you a way to retry history. Instead, they accept a narrower discipline: each will correct a false claim made in their own name, even when the claim flatters them. This is not renewed childhood trust. It is the beginning of accountability between people powerful enough to avoid it. The dream keeps its doors in the telling, and the dawn relinquishes its claim to illuminate events it never witnessed.
ba: Sanctuary and Stillness turn the conversation away from which sibling should have been thanked. Nythea recalls a kitchen assembled from several sleepers' memories, with three incompatible versions of the same table. Solarius remembers bread being shared behind a gate that remained shut. For a moment they almost make the resemblance into an absolution: both provided shelter, so perhaps neither needs to ask another difficult question. Your choices cannot honestly support that comfort.

Stillness leaves the missing seats visible. Sanctuary asks what the living needed after the immediate danger passed. Nythea admits that some people woke to homes that could no longer receive them. Solarius admits that keeping the world intact did not ensure it welcomed those survivors. They can neither rebuild those particular households here nor restore their lost years. They can stop calling survival the whole of rescue. Their first shared memory is not a heroic exchange across the breach, but the embarrassment of needing to be taught this by mortals. The siblings part without a promise that grief will diminish. They have agreed that a saved person may still arrive hungry, angry, or silent, and none of those arrivals cancels the duty to make room.
bb: Sanctuary and Defiance expose a tension the siblings cannot resolve by embracing. Solarius wants shelter to begin before a sufferer can prove deserving. Nythea has learned that shelter must also end when its occupant chooses, even if the keeper fears what waits beyond. He worries that an open door abandons the vulnerable. She worries that a closed door can teach its guardian to confuse obedience with safety.

They return to the mortal at the center of both concerns. Someone may need bread and still reject a god's account of how that bread became necessary. Someone may leave a dream and still grieve the comfort it provided. Neither sibling is entitled to make dependence into allegiance. Solarius admits that his seal was an act in a disaster, not a model for every later refuge. Nythea admits that escape alone cannot feed the person who has escaped. No new covenant alters your gifts or asks you to recruit anyone. This explicit conversation closes with a difficult courtesy: each sibling will hear a survivor refuse the other's protection without calling that refusal betrayal. They have not recovered the trust they once had. They have begun to imagine a trust that includes the freedom to depart.
